title: Neriage: layered clay colouring
subtitle: Stacking and throwing or hand-building with coloured clay layers to reveal patterns on cutting
excerpt: Neriage is a Japanese technique of stacking coloured clay layers and working them so the colours remain distinct in concentric or swirling patterns visible on the cut surface. When sliced, each piece reveals a cross-section of layered colour. The technique applies to wheel-thrown and hand-built forms.
sourceNotes: Neriage technique described from ceramic references. No single proprietary source.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Japanese clay technique of stacking coloured layers and building with them so each cut surface reveals the layered pattern
An inorganic mineral powder mixed into clay to produce colour; common examples include iron oxide (brown to black), cobalt carbonate (blue), and copper carbonate (green)

content.text: Metallic oxide colourants including cobalt, iron, copper, and manganese must be handled as dry powders with an FFP2 or N95 dust mask and gloves. Wash hands thoroughly after handling. Do not eat or drink in the clay colouring area. Fire with adequate kiln ventilation.

work, different coloured clay bodies are stacked and the stack is rolled, cut, re-stacked, and built into a form. The key rule is never to over-mix the colours: the layers should remain distinct all the way through the forming process.
are used to colour the clay in contrasting pairs: white and blue, white and brown, white and green.

materials.name: Clay coloured with cobalt carbonate (2%) or iron oxide (4%)
Transparent glaze for the finished piece

content.text: Wearing a dust mask, weigh the oxide powder and mix it into a small amount of water to form a paste. Knead the paste into the clay body thoroughly until the colour is even throughout. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes before using.

Roll each colour to 8 mm thick. Stack the slabs alternating colours: white, coloured, white, coloured, up to six layers. Compress the stack by rolling lightly across the top without distorting the layers.
Cut the stack in half and re-stack (the halves will double the number of colour layers). Repeat once more for fine layering. After two re-stacks the layers are 3 to 4 mm each.

For slab-built neriage: roll the stacked block into a slab 8 mm thick with the layers running horizontally through the thickness. Cut wall panels and base from this slab as normal. The cut edges will reveal the layer pattern.
For a twist or spiral pattern: take the stacked block and twist it once before rolling to a slab. The layers will spiral in cross-section.
After bisque fire, apply a thin transparent glaze to the piece. A thick glaze will obscure the clay layer pattern. Fire to the temperature appropriate to the clay body used.

items.problem: Layer pattern has blurred and the colours blended into a murky mid-tone
items.cause: Clay bodies were worked too much after stacking, or the two clay bodies had different moisture contents and the wetter clay distorted the drier one during working
items.fix: Match the moisture content of both clay colours before stacking: leave them both under a damp cloth for 30 minutes to equalise. After stacking, handle gently and avoid over-rolling

items.problem: Cracks develop at the edges of the slab during drying
items.cause: The two clay bodies have different shrinkage rates, causing stress at the layer boundaries
items.fix: Use the same base clay body for both colours, varying only the oxide. Dry slowly under a cloth cover to equalise the drying rate between the two coloured layers
